# Proposal: Automated Production Deployments

This proposal outlines a recommendation for reworking our production deployment
process. While I think it could be very valuable to rework our development
process as well, most changes to our developement process can happen
independently of changes to our production deployment process. Therefore, the
vast majority of suggested development process changes will be outlined in a
separate proposal.

## Motivation

Here's the current state of affairs:

All code for a client lives in a single Git repo. There is a folder for each
NetSuite account. In the case of Solution Source, that is a folder for
Production and a folder for Sandbox.

When writing code, we edit the files in the sandbox folder and upload to the sandbox account
as we work. When we are confident the code is working as it should, we get a
code review and commit our changes. When the time comes to deploy the code to
production, we first copy and paste the contents of all files changed in the sandbox to
the sister file in the production folder. Then we commit these changes. Finally,
we upload these updated files in the production folder to the production account
using the VS Code extension, or sometimes an Account Configuration Project (ACP). (Sometimes steps two and three
are swapped, but you get the idea.)

This has a few drawbacks:

1. We can never be confident that the code in our Git repos matches the code in
   the corresponding account. Finding code in an account that is not in source
   control is not uncommon. I also often forget to upload code changes made
   during a code review.
2. Leaving aside the process of actually uploading code, just moving code in our
   Git repos from sandbox to PROD is time-consuming and error prone.
3. We risk uploading code to the wrong account. It is up to individual developers
   to be careful enough to avoid taking down a production account with a bad
   upload.
4. It is easy to overwrite changes made by another developer to a file you are
   working on. Checking to make sure this doesn't happen is a time-consuming
   process, and not enforced.
5. If we want to introduce TypeScript, it isn't clear how we will add compilation
   to our process.
6. If we want to introduce tools such as a linter, a formatter, or a unit test
   framework, it's not clear how we would enforce running those tools before
   deployment, nor how to mandate that those checks pass before deployment.

## Proposed Process Change - Overview

### Git Repo Structure and Permissions

Every client will have one repo for their NetSuite code. Each repo will have one
branch for each account. I recommend:

-   `main` - Production account
-   `dev` - development sandbox
-   `test` - test sandbox, when applicable

This also means that we will no longer have "Client Name Sandbox" and
"Client Name Production" folders in our repos. Production code will live in the
production branch, development code will live in the development branch, etc.

Additionally, the branch for the production account (`main` in this example) will
have permissions set such that nobody can push directly to `main`, except perhaps
for select senior devs or SEs. Everybody else will need to open a pull request
in order to get their code changes into `main`.

### Development Process

For the purpose of this proposal, our development process would look almost
identical. Parts that are different are emphasized:

1. _Check out the correct branch (`dev`)_
2. Pull changes
3. Make your changes, and upload them to the dev sandbox using VS Code
4. When Changes are complete, get them code reviewed
5. _After code review, commit and push your changes to the `dev` branch_

The only difference here is that we are pulling from and pushing to the `dev`
branch instead of `main` or `master`.

### Deployment to Production

Every time code is pushed or merged into `main`, it will automatically be
deployed to the corresponding production account. This is the reason for the
branch restrictions on `main`. The vast majority of the time, we will want to
use PRs to move code from `dev` or `test` to `main`.

Here's a more detailed breakdown of the proposed process:

1. Open a PR from the `dev`(or `test`) branch to the `main` branch. Add
   any necessary documentation to the PR.
2. Run the following automated checks as soon as the PR is opened:
    1. Compare code in account with the code we deployed last. Also compare the
       last deployed script objects to the script objects in the account. They
       should be identical. If they are not, someone has made a chance directly
       in the production account and we should not deploy. Any conflicts will
       need to be resolved manually.
    2. (_optional_) Other checks can be inserted here later if desired. These could
       include unit tests and/or linter checks. The additional checks could also
       happen before the comparison if that makes more sense.
3. Request at least one review for the PR.
4. If the checks from step 2 pass and the PR has been approved, we can merge the
   code into `main`.
5. Merging code into `main` will trigger a deployment:
    1. Run the file compare check from step 2 again. Something could have
       changed between when we opened the PR and when we merge it. If the
       comparison finds conflicts, abort the deployment.
    2. Deploy the changes via ACP. This should include SuiteScript files and
       their corresponding objects.

## Proposed Process Change - Additional Details

### Git Repo

BitBucket and GitHub both allow you to disable pushing to specific branches.
I know BitBucket allows you to add exceptions for particular users, and I'd be
shocked if GitHub didn't also have that option. I would suggest that we only
allow a select few, if any, to push directly to main. This would allow more
senior devs to push quick fixes if necessary, but would require any other changes
to go through the standard review process.

### NetSuite Permissions

I'm not sure whether this is possible, but it would be good if we could revoke
token access to production accounts for devs. This would force us to go through
the process for deploying code to production.

This is a proposal that aims to move us one step closer to CI/CD at my job. I plan to pair it with a proposal for using Git + automated deployments as part of are development flow, but those change are out of scope for this proposal. I'm looking for feedback on how I could make this more compelling. Specifically, I'm looking for feedback on:

- Clarity and organization of ideas
- Objections or edge cases I may have missed
- Important details I have left out.

The plan is to present this to both the dev team and to the leadership team, since we will require a budget for the CI/CD tools.
Your proposal is well-structured and addresses many key points for improving the deployment process. Here's some feedback to make it more compelling:

1. Clarity and Organization:
   - The proposal is generally well-organized, but consider adding a brief executive summary at the beginning to highlight the main points and benefits.
   - Use more subheadings to break up large sections, especially in the "Proposed Process Change - Overview" section.

2. Potential Objections or Edge Cases:
   - Address the learning curve and potential initial slowdown as the team adapts to the new process.
   - Discuss how to handle hotfixes or emergency changes in production.
   - Consider the impact on client-specific customizations or configurations.

3. Additional Important Details:
   - Include a section on the expected benefits, such as improved reliability, reduced human error, and time savings.
   - Add a timeline for implementation and any associated costs.
   - Discuss the tools or services needed to implement this automated deployment process.
   - Include a section on rollback procedures in case of deployment failures.
   - Mention any necessary training or documentation for the team.

4. Strengthening the Proposal:
   - Provide concrete examples of how the new process would prevent past issues or improve specific scenarios.
   - Include metrics or KPIs to measure the success of the new process.
   - Address how this change aligns with broader company goals or industry best practices.
   - Discuss any potential risks and mitigation strategies.

5. Presentation Considerations:
   - For the leadership team, emphasize the business value, such as reduced downtime, improved security, and better resource allocation.
   - For the dev team, focus on how this will make their work easier and reduce stressful manual processes.

Overall, your proposal provides a solid foundation for improving the deployment process. Incorporating these suggestions should make it more comprehensive and persuasive to both technical and non-technical audiences.
